p: The letter names Paul. Most critical scholars think a later follower wrote it; others defend Paul.
b: The letter opens with Paul's name and was read as his from the second century on (Irenaeus quotes 1:4 as the words of "the apostle"). Since Friedrich Schleiermacher questioned it in 1807, most critical scholars have held that a follower wrote it in Paul's name after his death. P. N. Harrison's The Problem of the Pastoral Epistles (1921) argued from the vocabulary, much of which is rare in Paul and common in second-century writers. Among recent commentators, Luke Timothy Johnson (Anchor Bible) and Philip Towner (New International Commentary on the New Testament) argue for Paul as the author; I. Howard Marshall (International Critical Commentary) argues that Paul did not write it, and James Dunn treats it as written in Paul's name. The Plain follows the text and calls the writer Paul. The book page sets out the arguments, and the topic page on the Pastoral Letters gives each side's case and the debate over writing in another's name.

p: Paul's earlier letters call Christ Savior; the Pastorals give the title to God too, six times.
b: Elsewhere in Paul, sōtēr, "Savior," is rare and is said of Christ (Philippians 3:20; Ephesians 5:23). The three Pastoral Letters use it ten times, of God (1:1; 2:3; 4:10; Titus 1:3; 2:10; 3:4) and of Christ Jesus (2 Timothy 1:10; Titus 1:4; 2:13; 3:6). The idea has deep Jewish roots: Israel's God is "a God who is righteous and saves" (Isaiah 45:21). In the Greek cities it was also a title given to gods and to kings and emperors who were honored as rescuers, so calling God "our Savior" quietly claimed the title for him alone.

a: my true child in the faith
p: Gnēsios was the word for a legitimate child: Timothy is Paul's real heir in the faith.
b: Gnēsios means "born in wedlock, legitimate, genuine," and it was used for a child with a full right to inherit. Paul calls Timothy "my beloved and faithful child in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 4:17) and says that "as a child with a father" he served with Paul in the good news (Philippians 2:22). Acts first meets him already "a disciple" at Lystra (Acts 16:1), so "child" may mean that Paul brought him to faith or simply that Paul trained him. The phrase also tells the church that will hear the letter read that Timothy speaks with Paul's authority.

p: Paul's other greetings say "grace and peace"; the two letters to Timothy add mercy.
b: Paul's usual greeting joins the Greek "grace" (charis) and the Jewish greeting "peace" (shalom), as in Romans 1:7 and Ephesians 1:2. 1 and 2 Timothy add "mercy" (eleos, 2 Timothy 1:2), as Jude 2 does: "Mercy to you, and peace, and love" (Jude 1:2). In the Greek Old Testament eleos often renders hesed, God's loyal love. The word fits this letter, where Paul twice says "mercy was shown to me" (1:13, 16) and presents himself as the model of a sinner shown mercy.

p: Ephesus, the great port of Asia, was where Paul had worked for over two years (Acts 19).
b: Ephesus was the chief city of the Roman province of Asia, with a famous temple of Artemis (Acts 19:23-41). Paul taught there for more than two years (Acts 19:8-10) and later warned the Ephesian elders that men "out of your own group" would "say twisted things" (Acts 20:30), which is the very problem of this letter. The setting is hard to place in Acts. Acts 19:22 has Paul send Timothy ahead into Macedonia and stay in Asia himself, the reverse of 1:3. Those who hold that Paul wrote the letter usually place it after his release from Rome (Acts 28:30-31); others see the travel note as part of a later setting given to the letter.

p: The Greek begins "As I urged you..." and never finishes the thought; the Plain supplies "stay on".
b: Verses 3 and 4 in Greek are one long clause that starts "Just as I urged you to stay on in Ephesus..." and never reaches the main verb that should follow ("so now I urge you again"). Paul's letters do this elsewhere when he is dictating quickly (Galatians 2:4-6; Romans 5:12). The KJV adds "so do" at the end of 1:4 in italics to close the sentence. The Plain makes "stay on in Ephesus" a command, which is the clear sense.
orig: καθὼς παρεκάλεσά σε (kathōs parekalesa se), 'just as I urged you'

p: Who were these teachers? Jewish storytellers, early Gnostics, or both? The letter gives few clues.
b: The letter never sets out the false teaching in full; it gives hints. They want to be "teachers of the law" (1:7); they forbid marriage and some foods (4:3); Titus 1:14 speaks of "Jewish myths" and 2 Timothy 2:18 of a resurrection already past. Readers have proposed (1) Jewish speculation spun out of the family lists and stories of Genesis, like the retold Bible stories of the time; (2) an early form of the Gnostic systems of the second century, with their long chains of heavenly beings; (3) a mix of both. Irenaeus began his great attack on the Gnostics (about AD 180) by borrowing this verse: they bring in "vain genealogies, as the apostle says." See the note at 6:20.

p: Oikonomia is a household manager's plan. The KJV's "godly edifying" renders a different Greek word.
b: Oikonomia is the work of a household manager, and so a plan or arrangement; Ephesians uses it for God's plan to unite all things in Christ (Ephesians 1:10). Here the false teaching produces endless debate instead of serving "God's plan, which works by faith." The KJV has "godly edifying" and Young's Literal Translation "the building up of God," both renderings of a word for "building up" (oikodomia). Every edition in this site's word list, including the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus as the list gives it, reads oikonomia, and the Plain follows it. The other difference in this verse, "speculation" against "disputes," is set out in the variant.

p: "Conscience" comes six times in the three Pastorals: a good one keeps faith afloat (1:19).
b: Syneidēsis, the inner knowing that judges one's own acts, appears in 1:5, 19; 3:9; 4:2; 2 Timothy 1:3 and Titus 1:15. The letter ties it closely to faith: a "good" or "clean" conscience goes with sound faith (1:19; 3:9), and the false teachers have consciences "burned as if with a branding iron" (4:2). Paul uses the word often in Romans and 1 Corinthians, mostly of a conscience that can be weak or strong (Romans 14; 1 Corinthians 8-10); here it is a moral compass that a person can keep or throw away.

p: The word was used of Jewish teachers of the Torah, such as Gamaliel. Here it marks teachers inside the church.
b: Nomodidaskalos, "law-teacher," occurs only three times in the New Testament. Luke uses it of Jewish experts in the Torah (Luke 5:17) and of Gamaliel, who "taught the law, and the whole people honored him" (Acts 5:34). Here the teachers are inside the church and want that standing. So the problem seems to have a Jewish-Christian side: the law of Moses was being used for speculation (1:4) or for rules on food and marriage (4:3). Paul does not attack the law; he says it is good (1:8). His complaint is that these teachers do not understand it.

p: A play on words: the law (nomos) is good if used nomimōs, 'lawfully', in the way law is meant to be used.
b: The Greek repeats the root: kalos ho nomos ... nomimōs, "the law is good ... if used lawfully." Paul says the same thing in Romans: "the law is holy" (Romans 7:12). What is the lawful use? Verses 9 and 10 answer: law is aimed at wrongdoing, to restrain and expose it, not at the righteous person and not at myths and genealogies. Christian theology later built on this verse when it spoke of the "uses" of the law (to restrain evil, to show sin, to guide believers).

a: for those who kill their fathers or kill their mothers
t: A list shaped by the Ten Commandments?
p: Many commentators see the second half of the Ten Commandments behind the list; others find the match loose.
b: From the parent-killers on, many readers see the order of the second half of the Ten Commandments: honor your father and mother, do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness. Bengel wrote that Paul "names the unrighteous according to the order of the Decalogue"; Ellicott saw the list "following the order of the ancient Tables of Sinai"; Meyer thought Paul had the commandments in mind, "not adhering to it strictly." On this reading "slave dealers" stand for stealing, since the law punished stealing a person by death (Exodus 21:16; Deuteronomy 24:7). Others doubt the pattern. The Expositor's Greek Testament argues against it, noting that Paul puts adultery before murder when he lists the commandments in Romans 13:9; and the match is uneven, with two terms under adultery and none for coveting.

p: The same rare word as 1 Corinthians 6:9, rendered the same way; see the full note there.
b: Arsenokoitēs, made of "male" and "bed," occurs in the New Testament only here and in 1 Corinthians 6:9, and the Plain renders it the same way in both places. The note on 1 Corinthians 6:9 sets out the readings: a word coined from the Greek of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13 for sex between men, or a narrower word for exploitation. Here it stands between "those who commit sexual sin" and "slave dealers," a placement each side reads its own way (on whether the list follows the Ten Commandments, see the note at 1:9). The card on 1 Corinthians 6 gives the churches' teaching.

p: Andrapodistēs is one who captures or sells people into slavery; the KJV says 'menstealers'.
b: Andrapodistēs comes from andrapodon, a person taken as a slave, and named the kidnapper or the trader who made free people into slaves. The KJV renders it "menstealers." In the law of Moses this was a capital crime: "Whoever steals a person must be put to death, whether he has sold him or the person is found in his hand" (Exodus 21:16). The letter that later tells slaves to honor their masters (6:1-2) here lists the trade that made slaves among the lawbreakers, and readers on every side of later slavery debates have had to reckon with both.

p: Hygiainō is the word for being in good health; false teaching is a sickness in this letter.
b: Hygiainousa didaskalia is literally "healthy teaching"; the English word "hygiene" comes from the same root. The image runs through the Pastoral Letters: healthy words (6:3; 2 Timothy 1:13), being healthy in the faith (Titus 1:13; 2:2), the false teacher who is "sick" for arguments (6:4), and teaching that spreads "like gangrene" (2 Timothy 2:17). "Sound teaching" is the site's rendering in all three letters.

p: Euangelion, the word behind 'gospel'; here it is 'the good news of the glory of the blessed God'.
b: Euangelion means good news, a message worth announcing, and is the word behind English "gospel" (Old English god-spel, "good story"). This site renders it "the good news." "The blessed God" (makarios, happy, blessed) is a rare way to speak of God, found again in 6:15.

a: a man who blasphemed, persecuted and abused
p: Paul's own letters and Acts agree that he once hunted down the church.
b: Paul tells this part of his story in his own words: "I persecuted the church of God beyond all measure, and I was trying to wreck it" (Galatians 1:13). Acts says that "Saul was mauling the church" (Acts 8:3). The third word, hybristēs, names someone who treats others with violent contempt. Paul calls himself "the least of the apostles" for this reason (1 Corinthians 15:9). The memory here becomes a pattern for the whole church: if mercy reached him, it can reach anyone (1:16).

p: The law of Moses separated sins done unknowingly from sins done 'with a high hand' (Numbers 15).
b: Paul's plea that he acted "without knowing" echoes the law's difference between unintentional sins, for which there was atonement, and sins done defiantly (Numbers 15:22-31). Jesus prays from the cross, "Father, forgive them, because they do not know what they are doing" (Luke 23:34), and Peter tells the people of Jerusalem they acted in ignorance (Acts 3:17). Paul does not say ignorance made him innocent; he says it is why mercy was possible. He also gives the credit to grace (1:14), not to his ignorance.

p: A formula found five times in the Pastorals and nowhere else in the Bible; it points to a known saying.
b: Pistos ho logos appears in 1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11 and Titus 3:8, and the site renders it the same way each time. It seems to mark a saying already known in the churches, perhaps from teaching or worship, which the writer endorses. Here the saying clearly follows ("Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners"); in 3:1 and 4:9 readers argue whether it points forward or back. Twice (here and 4:9) it adds "and deserves full acceptance." The saying itself sounds like Jesus' own words: "The Son of Man came to look for what was lost and to save it" (Luke 19:10).

a: among them I am the first
p: Prōtos means first in order or first in rank: the worst sinner, or the first case of mercy?
b: Prōtos can mean first in time, first in rank, or foremost. Most translations take it as rank ("chief," KJV; "the worst"), Paul's sense of what persecuting the church had made him. But 1:16 repeats the word: mercy came "in me first," as a "pattern" for later believers, and that suggests first in order, the first great example. The two can stand together. The Plain keeps "first" in both verses so the reader can see the link. Note the present tense: "I am," not "I was."

a: To the King of the ages
p: Paul breaks into praise in the language of Israel's prayers: God the eternal King, unseen and one.
b: This doxology (a short burst of praise) uses Jewish ways of speaking of God. Psalm 145:13 says, "Your kingdom is a kingdom for all ages," and Jeremiah calls the LORD "the living God and a king who lasts forever" (Jeremiah 10:10). "The only God" echoes the Shema, "The LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4). "Cannot decay" is the word Paul uses for what the dead put on at the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:53), and "cannot be seen" matches Romans 1:20 and Colossians 1:15. A second, longer doxology closes the letter (6:15-16).

a: the prophecies spoken over you earlier
p: Prophets in the church seem to have pointed Timothy out for his work, as in Acts 13:1-3.
b: The letter twice mentions prophecy at the start of Timothy's ministry: here, and in 4:14, where the gift came "through a prophecy, with the laying on of the elders' hands." Acts shows the same pattern at Antioch, where the Holy Spirit spoke through prophets and teachers to set apart Barnabas and Saul, and they laid hands on them (Acts 13:1-3). Paul now uses those prophecies as encouragement: Timothy is not on this assignment by his own choice.

a: serve in the good campaign as a soldier
p: Strateuomai ... strateia: soldier's words. The Christian life is pictured as a military campaign.
b: The Greek repeats a root: strateuē ... tēn kalēn strateian, "serve as a soldier in the good campaign." The picture returns in 2 Timothy 2:3-4, where Timothy is called a good soldier of Christ Jesus. Paul uses soldier images elsewhere too (2 Corinthians 10:3-5; Ephesians 6:10-17). It is a different image from "the good contest" of 6:12, which comes from the games; the KJV's "fight the good fight" there has blurred the two for English readers.
orig: στρατεύῃ ... τὴν καλὴν στρατείαν (strateuē ... tēn kalēn strateian)

p: A sailor's image from a man who had been shipwrecked more than once.
b: Nauageō means to suffer shipwreck. Paul says he had been shipwrecked three times (2 Corinthians 11:25), and Acts 27 tells of a fourth on the way to Rome. A good conscience is pictured as part of the ship: throw it overboard, and faith breaks up. "Faith" here may be personal trust or "the faith" as a body of teaching; the Greek has the article ("the faith"), as often in these letters.

p: Two named teachers. 2 Timothy says Hymenaeus taught that the resurrection had already happened.
b: Hymenaeus appears again in 2 Timothy 2:17-18 with Philetus: they say "the resurrection has already happened," probably a purely spiritual resurrection at baptism. An Alexander "the coppersmith" did Paul great harm (2 Timothy 4:14), and an Alexander was pushed forward by the Jews in the Ephesian riot (Acts 19:33). Alexander was a very common name, and nothing settles whether any two of these are the same man. Naming names shows a real, local quarrel, whichever view of authorship is held.

p: The same phrase as 1 Corinthians 5:5: put out of the church, for the purpose of correction.
b: Paul used the same words of the man at Corinth: "hand such a man over to Satan, for the ruin of his flesh, so that on the day of the Lord his spirit may be saved" (1 Corinthians 5:5). Most readers take it as putting someone out of the church's fellowship into the world, where Satan rules (Ephesians 2:2), so that he will come to his senses. Others think of a sickness or other suffering that Paul expected to follow. Either way the goal is remedial: paideuō, "discipline, train," the word for bringing up a child. The church's discipline is not meant to destroy.

p: Four overlapping words for prayer; piling them up stresses how wide the church's prayer should be.
b: Deēseis are requests for a need; proseuchai is the general word for prayer to God; enteuxeis are petitions (Thayer's lexicon: "a petition, supplication," "used of prayer to God"); eucharistiai are thanksgivings. The pile of words stresses breadth, and the object stresses it more: "for every person." The church at prayer is to be as wide as God's will to save (2:4).

a: for kings and for all who hold high office
p: The exiles were told to pray for the city that held them. The church prays for the rulers of Rome.
b: Jeremiah told the exiles in Babylon: "Seek the peace of the city I sent you to as exiles, and pray for it to the LORD. When it has peace, you will have peace" (Jeremiah 29:7). The same logic is here: prayer for kings "so that we can spend calm and quiet lives." The ruler at the time was a pagan emperor. Praying for the emperor, rather than to him, was how Jews and Christians showed loyalty without joining the worship of the emperor. Romans 13:1-7 and 1 Peter 2:13-17 take the same line.

p: Eusebeia, reverence for God lived out, is a key word of the Pastorals: eight times in 1 Timothy, nine with the verb.
b: Eusebeia was a common Greek virtue: proper reverence toward the gods, and also toward parents, city and duty. Paul's earlier letters never use it; 1 Timothy has it eight times (2:2; 3:16; 4:7, 8; 6:3, 5, 6, 11), and 2 Timothy and Titus use it too (2 Timothy 3:5; Titus 1:1). Here it means faith in God shown in an ordered, decent life that outsiders can see and respect (3:7; 6:1). The verb in 5:4 ("practice godliness at home") makes nine. A different word, theosebeia, stands behind "honor God" in 2:10. The site renders the word "godliness" in all three letters.

a: He wants everyone to be saved
p: A key verse in the debate on election. Readers from Augustine to Wesley have taken 'everyone' differently.
b: The plain sense is that God wants every person saved, and the context (prayer "for every person," 2:1; a ransom "on behalf of all," 2:6) supports it. But if God wants it, why are not all saved? Chrysostom answered: "Because they would not: but His part was done." Augustine, in his Enchiridion (103), read "all" as "every sort of men" of every rank and circumstance, and Calvin wrote that the verse "relates to classes of men, and not to individual persons": no nation or rank, not even kings, is shut out. Wesley's note reads "Who willeth seriously all men," against any idea that God wants only a part. See the card.

t: The Shema in a new key
p: Israel's confession "The LORD is one" stands behind this verse, now joined to one mediator.
b: "Listen, Israel: The LORD is our God. The LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4) was the daily confession of Jewish faith. Paul uses it to make a point about the nations: because God is one, he is the God of Jews and Gentiles alike (Romans 3:29-30). Here the one God has one mediator, so the way to him is the same for every people, which is why the church prays for all (2:1) and Paul is a teacher "of the Gentiles" (2:7).

p: Mesitēs is a go-between who stands for both sides. Here the stress is that the mediator is human.
b: A mesitēs stood between two parties to make or guarantee an agreement. Paul calls Moses the mediator of the law (Galatians 3:19-20), and Hebrews calls Jesus the mediator of a new covenant (Hebrews 8:6; 9:15; 12:24). The Greek here repeats one word: the go-between of God and humans is himself human (anthrōpos). Chrysostom drew the conclusion that "a mediator ought to have communion with both parties," so that Christ, being man, was also God. The verse is also central to the question whether the saints may pray for us without taking from Christ's place: see the card.

a: a ransom on behalf of all
p: A Greek form of Jesus' own words in Mark 10:45, with 'many' turned into 'all'.
b: Jesus said he came "to give his life as a ransom in place of many" (Mark 10:45). Here the saying is recast in smoother Greek: antilytron (a compound, "ransom in exchange") hyper pantōn, "on behalf of all." In Hebrew idiom "many" often means the whole multitude, so "all" may be a faithful gloss on Jesus' words. A ransom was the price paid to free a prisoner or slave. The image of whom the price was paid to was argued over for centuries; see the topic page on the atonement.

a: the witness to this given when its time came
p: Three Greek words, 'the witness, in its own times': the cross itself was God's testimony, given on time.
b: The Greek is only to martyrion kairois idiois, "the testimony, in its own seasons." It probably means that Christ's self-giving was God's testimony to his will to save all, given at the moment God chose (compare Galatians 4:4, "when the time had come to its fullness"). Some take it as the apostles' witness to that event, carried on "at the proper times" by Paul (2:7). The same phrase "in its own times" returns at 6:15 and Titus 1:3.

p: Jews and early Christians usually prayed standing, with arms lifted, not kneeling with folded hands.
b: Raised hands were the common posture of prayer in Israel and the ancient world: "my hands raised high as the evening grain offering" (Psalm 141:2). The praying figure with arms spread wide, called the orans, is a common image in early Christian art. "Holy" hands are clean hands, a picture from Psalm 24:3-4 of the worshiper who has not done wrong. Anger and argument spoil prayer, as Jesus also taught (Matthew 5:23-24; Mark 11:25).

p: Dialogismos is reasoning, and so either quarreling or inner doubt. The KJV has 'doubting'.
b: Dialogismos is reasoning or a train of thought, and so either an argument with others or a debate inside oneself. The KJV and the World English Bible read "doubting," the American Standard Version "disputing" and the Berean Standard Bible "dissension." Set beside "anger," the Plain takes it as quarreling: prayer free of strife with others. The other reading makes it prayer free of doubt toward God. The false teachers' love of "arguments and word-fights" (6:4) favors the first.

p: Elaborate braids, gold and pearls were marks of wealth and status, not only of beauty.
b: In the Roman world, elaborate hair styles woven with gold, and pearls, were the look of rich women, shown off in public. Moral writers, pagan and Jewish, warned that a good wife's beauty was her character, not her jewelry, and 1 Peter 3:3-4 makes the same point. In a church that met in homes and included slaves and the poor, such display could also shame poorer sisters. The concern is less about fashion than about worship, money and rank (compare 6:9, 17).

p: Hēsychia means calm and quiet, the same root as the 'quiet lives' of 2:2; Greek has another verb for keeping silent.
b: Hēsychia is quietness, a calm and peaceable bearing; the related adjective described the "quiet lives" all believers should lead (2:2). Greek has another word for keeping silent, the verb sigaō (1 Corinthians 14:28, 30, 34). So many readers think the verse asks for a calm, receptive manner rather than total silence; others note that in 2:12 it is set against teaching, so it includes not taking the teacher's role. Notice too that the command is that a woman learn: women as students of Scripture were not taken for granted in that world (compare Mary "at Jesus' feet," Luke 10:39). The verse does not say to whom the "submission" is owed; possibilities readers raise include the teaching, the church's order, or a husband.

a: to hold authority over a man
p: This verb appears only here in the Bible. Its meaning, neutral or negative, is at the center of the debate.
b: Authenteō occurs nowhere else in the New Testament or the Greek Old Testament, and its meaning has been argued since the 1980s. Al Wolters' study of the word family (2000) found that the noun authentēs had three distinct senses in ancient Greek, "murderer," "master" and "doer"; the question is which of them the verb builds on. Readers take it as (1) neutral "exercise authority" (George Knight, 1984, the complementarian reading); (2) a negative "domineer" or "assume, usurp authority" (the KJV's "usurp"; the Assemblies of God writer George P. Wood, who prefers "to assume or usurp authority"), so that only a wrong kind of authority is barred; (3) "proclaim herself the author of man" (Richard and Catherine Kroeger, 1992, tied to a myth that Eve came first). H. Scott Baldwin's survey (1995) lists the attested senses. The Plain's "hold authority over" is closest to reading (1); the gloss on it names the others, and the choice among them is the heart of the debate.

a: I do not allow a woman to teach
t: A rule for that church, or for every church?
p: Is this a local rule for Ephesus, a rule tied to a lack of training, or a lasting rule from creation?
b: Readers divide on how far 2:12 reaches. (1) A lasting rule: the reason given in 2:13 is creation itself, not a local problem, so the teaching and governing office of the church belongs to men (Calvin: the office "which God has committed to men only"; the Danvers Statement, affirmation 6; the Baptist Faith and Message 2000). (2) A local rule: the letter fights false teaching that had spread through households (5:13; 2 Timothy 3:6-7), women had not yet been taught ("let a woman learn," 2:11), and Paul elsewhere names women as coworkers and has women pray and prophesy (Romans 16:1-7; 1 Corinthians 11:5). Wesley glossed it "by public teaching." The card sets out the churches' positions.

p: Paul's verb is the one the Greek of Genesis 2:7 uses: God shaped the man from dust.
b: Genesis says, "the LORD God shaped the man from dust of the ground" (Genesis 2:7), and only later "built the rib he had taken from the man into a woman" (Genesis 2:22). The Greek of Genesis 2:7 uses plassō, "shape, mold," the verb used here. Paul argues from the same order in 1 Corinthians 11:8-9, though he adds there that "man comes through woman" (1 Corinthians 11:12). Readers who take 2:12 as lasting see the creation order as its ground; others take 2:13-14 as an example drawn from the story (Eve was taught second-hand and was deceived), suited to women who had not yet learned.

p: Eve said, "The snake fooled me" (Genesis 3:13). Paul elsewhere lays the fall at Adam's door.
b: The verb is the one Eve uses in the Greek of Genesis: "The snake fooled me, and I ate" (Genesis 3:13), with an added prefix here, "fooled through and through." 2 Corinthians 11:3 uses the same picture for the whole church: "the snake fooled Eve with his cunning." Yet in Romans Paul says "sin entered the world through one man" (Romans 5:12), Adam, not Eve. So 2:14 does not claim Adam was less guilty; it says he sinned knowingly. Chrysostom took it to mean that "the woman taught the man once," with disastrous results. Others read it as a warning about being deceived by false teachers, which the letter fears for the whole church (4:1).

a: she will be saved through the bearing of children
p: One of the hardest lines in Paul. Five main readings, from the birth of the Messiah to safety in labor.
b: (1) Through the Child. The Greek has the article, "through the childbearing," and some read it as the birth of the Messiah, the offspring promised to the woman in Genesis 3:15, where the Greek even says "he" will watch for the snake's head. (2) Kept safe in childbirth. Sōzō can mean rescue from danger; Wesley: "Carried safe through the pain and danger." (3) Through her ordinary calling. Chrysostom took it of raising children ("by means of children"); Calvin said it shows the path, not the cause, of salvation. (4) Against the false teachers, who forbade marriage (4:3): bearing children is no bar to salvation. (5) Against Artemis: Sandra Glahn (2023) points out that Ephesian women looked to Artemis as helper in childbirth. "She" moves from Eve to women in general, and "they" (see the next note) widens it again.

p: The verb is plural after a singular 'she'. Women in general, mothers and their children, or husband and wife?
b: Greek changes from "she will be saved" to "if they stay." Most readers take "they" as women in general, the class Eve stands for. Chrysostom took it as the children: mothers are saved "if after childbearing, they keep them in charity and purity." A few take it as husband and wife together. The conditions (faith, love, holiness, good sense) are the same ones the letter asks of every believer, which shows that the verse does not make childbearing a way of earning salvation.

p: Episkopos means overseer; English 'bishop' comes from it. Here it may be the same office as 'elder'.
b: Episkopē is the post of an episkopos, an "overseer" or supervisor; through Latin episcopus the word became English "bishop." In Acts, Paul calls the Ephesian elders "overseers" (Acts 20:17, 28), and Titus 1:5-7 moves from "elders" to "the overseer" as if they were one office. Here 3:2 speaks of "the overseer" in the singular, perhaps meaning any overseer, and 5:17 speaks of "elders who lead." Whether bishops are a separate order above elders is the dividing question of church order: see the card. The letters of Ignatius of Antioch, traditionally dated about AD 108 (some scholars place them later), show the next stage, with one overseer over the elders in each city.

p: Literally 'a one-woman man.' No polygamy? No remarriage? A faithful husband? Must he be married?
b: The Greek is mias gynaikos andra, "of one woman a man," and the Plain keeps it literal so every reading stays open. (1) No polygamy: Chrysostom says Paul writes it "as prohibiting his having more than one" wife, not as a rule that he must have one. (2) No remarriage after divorce. (3) No second marriage at all, even after a wife's death; the matching "wife of one husband" (5:9) points this way. (4) A faithful husband, the sense many modern translations give. (5) Married, a reading Wesley rejected: it "neither means that a bishop must be married, nor that he may not marry a second wife," but bars polygamy and easy divorce. See the card on celibacy.

p: Philoxenos, 'stranger-loving'. Churches met in homes, and travelers depended on believers' houses.
b: Philoxenos means loving strangers, and the Plain renders it as Titus 1:8 does. In a world of poor inns, Christian travelers, teachers and messengers needed homes that would take them in (3 John 5-8; Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2), and the church itself met in households. An overseer's house was in effect a church building, which is why his household matters so much in this list (3:4-5).

p: Managing a household and caring for a church are the same kind of work: the church is God's family.
b: Paul argues from the smaller to the larger: a man who cannot lead his own home cannot look after God's. The church met in houses (Romans 16:5; Philemon 2), had masters and slaves, parents and children, and widows, and this letter treats it as God's household throughout (3:15). The verb for "look after" (epimeleomai) is the one used of the Samaritan who took care of the wounded man (Luke 10:34-35).

p: Either the judgment the devil fell under through pride, or a charge brought by 'the slanderer'.
b: To krima tou diabolou can mean the judgment that came on the devil, whose pride was traditionally his downfall, or a judgment brought about by the devil. Diabolos literally means "slanderer, accuser," and the next verse speaks of shame before outsiders and "the devil's snare." In 3:11 the same word, in the plural, is used of human beings: women who are "not given to slander" are literally "not devils."

p: Diakonos means servant, helper or agent. Here, beside the overseers, it names an office.
b: Diakonos is an ordinary word for a servant, attendant or go-between. Paul often uses it of himself and others as servants of Christ (4:6, "a good servant of Christ Jesus"). Where it stands next to the overseers as a second group with its own qualifications, as here and in Philippians 1:1, it names an office, "deacons." The text never says what deacons did. The Seven of Acts 6 are often taken as the first deacons, but Acts does not call them that. Romans 16:1 calls Phoebe "a servant of the church in Cenchreae" with the same word.

p: Mystērion: God's secret plan, now told. Deacons must hold the faith, not just serve tables.
b: In Paul a mystērion is a secret of God that has now been made known (Romans 16:25-26; Ephesians 3:3-6), not a puzzle. "The mystery of the faith" is the good news about Christ, and 3:16 gives a short form of it, "the mystery of godliness." Deacons are not asked to teach (unlike overseers, 3:2), but they must hold the faith firmly and with a clean conscience.

p: The Greek says only 'women likewise', in the middle of the rules for deacons. Two readings.
b: Gynaikas hōsautōs, "women likewise." Gynē means both "woman" and "wife." (1) Deacons' wives: the KJV supplies "their wives," and some note that 3:12 returns to male deacons. (2) Women deacons: there is no "their" in the Greek; "likewise" introduces a new group in the same way as in 3:8; the list is the same kind of list as the deacons' ("serious" opens both); no rules are given for overseers' wives. Phoebe is called diakonos of her church (Romans 16:1). Pliny, governor of Bithynia, writes that he questioned under torture two slave women "who were called ministrae" (Letters 10.96.8: ex duabus ancillis, quae ministrae dicebantur). The Latin word means female attendants or servants; some translators render it "deaconesses," and whether it names a church office is debated. Chrysostom: "He is speaking of those who hold the rank of Deaconesses." See the card.

p: Bathmos means a step. A step up to a higher office, or a good standing before God and the church?
b: Bathmos, found only here in the New Testament, is a step or stair, and so a grade or standing. Some later readers took it as a step up from deacon to a higher office. Most modern readers take it as a good standing, respect in the church and confidence before God, which fits the "boldness" that follows. Parrēsia is the freedom to speak openly, the opposite of shame.

p: The key image of the letter: the church is God's household, with order, family and duties.
b: Oikos theou can mean God's house, a temple, or God's household, a family. The letter means both, but the family is in front: older men as fathers, older women as mothers (5:1-2), widows cared for (5:3-16), slaves and masters (6:1-2), and the overseer as a household manager (3:4-5). The word behind "God's plan" in 1:4, oikonomia, is built on the same root, oikos, "house." Ephesians 2:19-22 joins the two pictures: God's household and a holy temple.

a: a pillar and a firm base for the truth
t: The pillar and base of the truth
p: The church holds up the truth. Does that give it authority over teaching, or make it truth's servant?
b: A stylos is a pillar, and a hedraiōma a foundation or support. The Greek has no article, "a pillar and base," and the image is that the church holds the truth up and keeps it steady in the world. Catholic and Orthodox teaching cite the verse for the church's role in guarding and teaching the faith. Protestant confessions answer that Scripture judges the church's teaching: the Westminster Confession names "the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture" as the supreme judge (1.10). Wesley attached the words to what follows: the mystery of godliness is "the foundation and support of all the truth taught in his church." See the card.

p: Homologoumenōs: 'as all agree, admittedly.' It introduces words the church already confessed.
b: Homologoumenōs means "confessedly, beyond dispute," from homologeō, "to confess" (as in "the good confession," 6:12-13). It introduces what is widely held to be a fragment of an early hymn or creed: six short lines, each a verb in the same form with a phrase. The lines may move in pairs between earth and heaven: flesh and Spirit, angels and nations, world and glory. Compare the other early confessions of Christ in Philippians 2:6-11 and Colossians 1:15-20.

p: Edikaiōthē, 'was justified': shown to be in the right, most likely by the resurrection.
b: Edikaiōthē is the verb Paul uses for "justify": to declare someone in the right. Here it means that Jesus, condemned by people "in the flesh," was shown to be in the right by God. Most readers see the resurrection behind it, as in Romans 1:4, where he "was marked out as Son of God with power by his resurrection from the dead" (Romans 1:4). En pneumati may be "in the Spirit" (God's Spirit) or "in spirit" (his spiritual, risen life), contrasted with "in the flesh." The Plain capitalizes Spirit, with most translations.

p: The verb Acts uses of the Ascension: 'the day he was taken up' (Acts 1:2).
b: Anelēmphthē, "was taken up," is the verb Luke uses for the Ascension: "until the day he was taken up" (Acts 1:2; also Acts 1:11, 22). The hymn's last line, then, is the Ascension, though it comes after "believed in the world," which shows that the hymn is not in time order. The Greek Old Testament uses the same verb for Elijah, taken up to heaven (2 Kings 2:11).

p: Is this the end of history, or the writer's own day? The letter treats the warning as already coming true.
b: The Spirit's warning sounds like a prophecy about the far future, but the letter treats it as present: Timothy must deal with these teachers now (4:6-7). Early Christians believed the "last days" had begun with Jesus (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2), and Jesus himself had warned of false prophets (Mark 13:22). In Acts, Paul tells the Ephesian elders: "out of your own group men will stand up and say twisted things, so they can pull the disciples away to follow them" (Acts 20:30). Readers in every century since have applied the verse to the teachers of their own time.

p: Strict teachers banned marriage and some foods. Who were they? Several kinds of ascetics fit.
b: The letter does not name them, but several groups of the time would fit. Some Jewish-Christian teachers kept food laws and fasts as a path to holiness (Colossians 2:16-23). Some believers thought that, since the resurrection had come (2 Timothy 2:18), marriage belonged to the old age (compare Luke 20:35). In the second century, some Christian stories, such as the Acts of Paul and Thecla, show Paul praising virginity above marriage, and Dennis MacDonald argued (1983) that the Pastorals were written to answer that kind of story. Whoever they were, the letter answers with creation: what God made is good (4:4).

a: Every created thing God made is good
t: Creation is good, and grace before meals
p: The answer to the ascetics is Genesis 1: 'there it was, very good.' Food received with thanks is holy.
b: The verse echoes the refrain of creation: "God looked at everything he had made, and there it was, very good" (Genesis 1:31). Jesus had declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), and Paul wrote that "nothing is common in itself" (Romans 14:14). Verse 5 says food is made holy "by God's word and prayer," which fits the Jewish custom of blessing God before eating, often with words from Scripture: the blessing does not change the food but receives it as God's gift. Christians have said grace at meals ever since.

p: The Greek is the plural 'brothers,' used of a mixed group. The Plain keeps it, as in Romans and Acts.
b: The Greek adelphoi is the masculine plural, and Greek used it for a mixed group; here Paul means all the believers, women and men, whom Timothy is to teach. This site renders it "brothers" in Romans, Acts and the other letters, with this note at first use in each book (see the note at Romans 1:13). The word itself carries the letter's main picture: the church is a family, God's household (3:15; 5:1-2).

a: the kind of tales old women tell
p: Graōdēs, 'old-womanish', was a stock put-down for silly stories. The KJV: 'old wives' fables'.
b: Graōdeis mythous are "old-womanish myths," a common Greek scornful phrase for stories told to children by old nurses, not worth an adult's belief. The KJV's "old wives' fables" gave English its "old wives' tale." The phrase is an insult of its time, and it is aimed at the myths (1:4), not at older women, whom the letter honors (5:2). Some scholars, noting that women carried such teaching from house to house (5:13; 2 Timothy 3:6), think the stories were spread among women, perhaps legends like those later written down in the Acts of Paul and Thecla.

p: The Greek city had its gymnasium; Paul borrows the trainer's language for godliness.
b: "Train" (4:7) and "exercise" here are gymnazō and gymnasia, the words of the gymnasium, the center of a Greek city's education and athletics. Paul does not despise exercise; it brings "a little benefit" (or benefit "for a little while"). But godliness is training with a promise for both lives, this one and the age to come. Paul uses athletic images often (1 Corinthians 9:24-27; 2 Timothy 2:5; 4:7).

a: He is Savior of all people, most of all of believers
p: If God is Savior of all people, are all saved? Readers have answered in several ways.
b: The verse puzzles every reader. (1) All will be saved in the end, believers first: the verse has been a text for Christian universalists. (2) Savior in two senses: God preserves and provides for all people in this life, and saves believers for eternity. (3) Savior of all in offer, of believers in fact: Christ's ransom is "on behalf of all" (2:6) and God wants all saved (2:4), but salvation is received by faith. (4) "That is": some take malista as "namely," so "Savior of all people, that is, of believers." The verse goes with 2:4-6, and the churches' answers are on the card there.

p: Timothy had worked with Paul for many years, yet was still young beside the elders he was to lead.
b: Neotēs, "youth," was used in Greek of a fairly wide span of adult life. Timothy had joined Paul on his second journey (Acts 16:1-3), so by the time of this letter he had been in ministry for years; but in a culture that gave authority to age, he was younger than many of the elders he had to correct (5:1, 19-20). Paul's answer is not to claim rank but to be a model: speech, life, love, faith, purity.

p: The synagogue read the Law and the Prophets aloud each Sabbath. The church took over the practice.
b: Anagnōsis is "reading," here reading aloud in the gathering. In the synagogue the Scriptures were read and then explained: "When the Law and the Prophets had been read, the synagogue leaders sent someone to tell them, 'Brothers, if any of you has a word to encourage the people, speak up'" (Acts 13:15). The same three steps appear here: reading, urging (the same word as "encourage" in Acts 13:15, paraklēsis), teaching. Paul's own letters were read aloud too (Colossians 4:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:27).
r: Acts 13:15; Luke 4:16-21; Acts 15:21; Colossians 4:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:27; Nehemiah 8:8

a: the laying on of the elders' hands
p: Here the elders laid hands on Timothy; in 2 Timothy 1:6 it is Paul's hands. Ordination, then and now.
b: Moses laid his hands on Joshua to pass on his charge (Numbers 27:18-23), and the church at Antioch laid hands on Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:3). Presbyterion, "body of elders," is the word Luke uses for the Jewish council of elders in Jerusalem (Luke 22:66; Acts 22:5). 2 Timothy 1:6 speaks of "the laying on of my hands": Paul and the elders together, or two different moments. Churches differ on what this act is. The Catholic Catechism teaches that the apostles "by the imposition of hands ... passed on to their auxiliaries the gift of the Spirit" (1556; its footnote points to this verse), in the sacrament of Holy Orders; most Protestant churches count two sacraments only and see ordination as a solemn rite of prayer and recognition. See the card.

p: Salvation is God's gift (1:15), yet Timothy 'saves' himself and his hearers by holding to the teaching.
b: The same letter that says Christ came "to save sinners" (1:15) here tells Timothy that by keeping at the teaching he "will save" himself and his hearers. The verb is the ordinary one for salvation. Paul does not mean that Timothy earns salvation; he means that faithfulness to the good news is the path by which God saves, and that a teacher who drifts takes his hearers with him (compare 2:15; Philippians 2:12-13). Churches that debate whether believers can fall away read this verse too.

p: Presbyteros means an older man and also a church elder. Here, beside 'younger men,' it means age.
b: Presbyteros is the comparative of "old": an older man. It is also the title of the church's elders (5:17, 19). Here it is paired with "younger men," and then with older and younger women, so it means age. Later in the chapter (5:17-19) the same word names the office. The overlap is natural: the leaders of Jewish towns and synagogues were "the elders," usually older men of standing.

p: Timaō means to honor, but here, as in 5:17, honor includes money: support.
b: Timē means "honor" and also "price, value"; the verb timaō can mean to give honor in a concrete way. The rest of the passage is about who should support widows (5:4, 8, 16), so "give honor" includes material support, as "double honor" for elders includes pay (5:17-18). Jesus used "honor your father and mother" in the same sense, for supporting parents (Mark 7:10-12).

a: the widows who are widows in fact
p: The Law of Moses made widows God's special concern; the first church fed its widows daily (Acts 6:1).
b: In the ancient world a widow without a son or a family usually had no income. The Law of Moses names the widow, the orphan and the foreigner again and again as people God protects (Exodus 22:22-24; Deuteronomy 14:29; 24:17-21), and the prophets judge Israel by how it treats them (Isaiah 1:17). The church in Jerusalem fed its widows daily (Acts 6:1), and James calls care for widows and orphans pure religion (James 1:27). This chapter sorts out a practical problem: with many widows and limited money, the church supports those with no family, and families support their own.
r: Exodus 22:22-24; Deuteronomy 14:29; Deuteronomy 24:17-21; Acts 6:1; James 1:27; Isaiah 1:17

p: The Greek says 'let them learn': the children and grandchildren, or the widows themselves?
b: "Let them learn" is plural. Most readers take the subject as the children and grandchildren, who are to repay their parents by caring for them. A few take it as widows in general, who should practice godliness at home and repay their own parents. The Plain takes the majority view. "Practice godliness" is the verb of eusebeia (2:2): godliness begins with family duty, as the commandment to honor parents shows.

a: Put a widow on the list
p: The church kept a roll of widows, over sixty, with a record of good works: a recognized group.
b: Katalegesthō means "let her be enrolled." The church kept a list, and enrollment had conditions: age sixty or more, married once ("the wife of one husband," the same form as the overseers' "husband of one wife," 3:2), and a known record of service. 5:11-12 implies that enrolled widows made a pledge, perhaps not to marry again. So the list seems to have been more than a poor roll: an order of widows devoted to prayer (5:5) and good works, something like the later orders of widows and deaconesses in the early church.

a: washed the feet of the saints
p: Washing guests' feet was a slave's task; Jesus did it and told his disciples to do the same.
b: Washing a guest's dusty feet was a basic act of hospitality (Genesis 18:4; Luke 7:44), usually done by a slave. Jesus did it for his disciples and said, "I am the Lord and the Teacher, and I washed your feet. So you too owe it to one another to wash each other's feet" (John 13:14). Here it stands for humble service to traveling and visiting believers. "The saints" are God's holy people, all believers, not a special class.

a: when sexual desire sets them at odds with Christ
p: A rare verb for the pull of sexual desire. A pledge to Christ is set against a new marriage.
b: Katastrēniaō is a rare verb; Thayer's lexicon defines it "to feel the impulses of sexual desire," with "of Christ" meaning "to one's loss" (the KJV's "wax wanton against Christ"). The Plain keeps both parts: the desire, and its turning against Christ. The picture is a widow enrolled with a pledge to serve Christ (5:12, "their first pledge," literally "their first faith") who then wants to marry and so breaks the pledge. Paul does not call marriage a sin; in 5:14 he wants the younger widows to marry. The problem is a broken promise, and perhaps marriage to an unbeliever (1 Corinthians 7:39). Others read "first faith" as faith in Christ itself, abandoned for a pagan marriage.

t: Gossips and meddlers, or dabblers in magic?
p: Periergoi means busybodies; in Acts 19:19 the same word names the magic arts practiced at Ephesus.
b: Phlyaroi are people who talk nonsense, and periergoi are busybodies who meddle in what is not theirs. But ta perierga is also a Greek term for magic, used at Ephesus itself: "Quite a few of those who had practiced magic gathered up their books" (Acts 19:19). So a few readers think the young widows going from house to house were carrying not just gossip but the false teaching (4:1; 2 Timothy 3:6) or magical lore. Most take the plainer sense: idle talk that damages others.

p: 1 Corinthians 7 says a widow is happier if she stays single; here young widows should marry.
b: In 1 Corinthians 7:39-40 Paul allows a widow to marry "only in the Lord" but thinks she is happier staying as she is; here he wants younger widows to marry and have children. Readers who hold that Paul wrote both explain the difference by the situation: at Corinth, an expected crisis (1 Corinthians 7:26); at Ephesus, idle young widows drawn into false teaching (5:13, 15) and teachers who forbade marriage (4:3). Critical scholars count it among the signs of a later writer, for whom settled households had become the church's defense. Either way, the reason given is public: no opening for the opponent to slander the church.

p: Timē is honor and also price or pay. The next verse, about wages, shows that support is meant.
b: Diplēs timēs, "double honor," is followed at once by two sayings about a worker's pay (5:18), so it includes material support. Readers differ on "double": respect and pay together; twice what widows received (5:3, where the same word is used); or simply generous honor. The elders "who lead well" (proestōtes, the verb of 3:4-5, leading a household) are one group; "above all those who toil at the word and at teaching" may be a subgroup. Presbyterian church order distinguishes "teaching elders" and "ruling elders" within the one office of elder (Presbyterian Church in America, Book of Church Order 7-2).

t: Deuteronomy and a saying of Jesus, both 'Scripture'
p: Two quotations: the ox (Deuteronomy 25:4) and 'A worker has earned his pay,' word for word Luke 10:7.
b: The first quotation is Deuteronomy 25:4, "Do not muzzle an ox while it is threshing" (Deuteronomy 25:4), which Paul also used for apostles' support: "You shall not muzzle an ox that is treading out the grain" (1 Corinthians 9:9). The second matches Jesus' words in Luke exactly in the Greek: "a worker has earned his pay" (Luke 10:7); Matthew's form has "food" (Matthew 10:10). Readers differ: (1) "Scripture" covers both, so a Gospel saying, or Luke's Gospel itself, was already ranked with the Law, a point used to date the letter later; (2) "Scripture" governs only the first quotation, and the second is a known saying of Jesus (compare 1 Corinthians 9:14); (3) it was a common proverb that Jesus also used.
r: Deuteronomy 25:4; 1 Corinthians 9:9; Luke 10:7; Matthew 10:10; 1 Corinthians 9:14; 2 Peter 3:16

a: on the word of two or three witnesses
p: The rule of Deuteronomy 19:15, which Jesus and Paul both apply in the church.
b: Deuteronomy's rule protected anyone accused: "A matter is to stand on the word of two witnesses or on the word of three witnesses" (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jesus applied it to correcting a brother, "so that every statement may stand on the word of two or three witnesses" (Matthew 18:16), and Paul to his own dealings with Corinth (2 Corinthians 13:1). Leaders draw accusations, and this guards them from one person's grudge; but 5:20-21 forbids covering up when the charge is proved.

p: Angels as witnesses of judgment; 'chosen' may set them apart from the angels who fell.
b: Angels appear in the Bible as witnesses of the heavenly court (Luke 9:26; 12:8-9; Revelation 14:10). "Chosen" or "elect" angels may be those God has chosen for his service, or those who stayed loyal, in contrast to the angels who sinned (Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4). The solemn oath shows how seriously Paul takes fairness in church discipline: "doing nothing by leaning to one side."

a: Put your hands on no one in haste
p: Most take this as ordaining elders too quickly; some as receiving back sinners too quickly.
b: Coming after the instructions on elders (5:17-21) and recalling 4:14, the verse most likely warns against ordaining an elder before he has been tested (compare 3:6, 10). If Timothy does, he shares the blame for that man's sins. Some readers, ancient and modern, take it as the laying on of hands to restore a sinner who has repented, since 5:20 speaks of sinners rebuked in front of the church. The next verses (5:24-25), on sins that show only later, fit either reading.

p: Advice about health: wine was a common medicine. The verse became a battleground in temperance debates.
b: The verse breaks into the charge with personal advice. Timothy may have drunk only water out of strictness, perhaps to keep clear of the teachers' charges, or of their asceticism (4:3). Wine was a common medicine in the ancient world (Luke 10:34), and much water was unsafe. Later the verse was argued over. When the American temperance movement turned against all alcohol, some churches replaced wine with grape juice; in 1869 Thomas Welch, a communion steward at the Methodist church in Vineland, New Jersey, troubled by serving wine at Communion, began bottling unfermented grape juice. Advocates of total abstinence read the verse as medicine only; others, as a sign that drinking in moderation is no sin. See the topic page on wine.

a: Those who are slaves under a yoke
p: The Ephesian church included slaves and masters. Paul does not call for freeing them here.
b: The church had both slaves and masters in it. "Under a yoke" is the language of hard labor. The reason Paul gives is the church's witness: slaves who scorned their masters would bring God's name into contempt (compare Titus 2:9-10). Paul does not call for an end to slavery here, unlike 1 Corinthians 7:21, where, on the reading this site's Plain follows, he tells a slave to take freedom if he can (the note there gives the other reading), and Philemon, where he asks for Onesimus to be received "as a brother." The same letter lists slave dealers among lawbreakers (1:10). Later readers, from defenders of slavery to abolitionists, have weighed these texts against each other.

a: the masters who gain from their good work
p: The Greek can mean the masters who receive the slaves' good service, or masters who devote themselves to kindness.
b: Hoi tēs euergesias antilambanomenoi is unclear. Euergesia was the word for a public benefaction, the good deeds of a patron. (1) Most take it as the masters who "receive the benefit" of the slaves' service, which is the Plain's reading. (2) Others take antilambanomai in its other sense, "devote oneself to," so that the masters are those who "devote themselves to kindness" toward their slaves; then the slaves serve masters who are themselves doing good. Either way, faith in the same Lord does not cancel the slave's duty, but makes it service to a brother.

a: godliness is a source of profit
p: Porismos, a means of gain. The teachers make godliness pay; 6:6 turns the word around.
b: Porismos is a means of making a living or a profit. Traveling teachers who charged fees were common in the Greek world, and Paul was careful to support himself so that no one could say he preached for money (1 Thessalonians 2:5, 9; 2 Corinthians 2:17). The teachers in Ephesus apparently made money from their teaching (Titus 1:11 says the same of teachers on Crete). Verse 6 turns the word around: godliness is a great source of profit, but only with contentment.

a: when it comes with being content
p: Autarkeia, 'self-sufficiency': a key Stoic virtue, which Paul turns into trust in God.
b: Autarkeia was a favorite virtue of the Stoic and Cynic philosophers: being self-sufficient, needing little, untouched by fortune. Paul uses the word of himself in Philippians 4:11, where he says he has learned to be content in any state, and he names the source of that strength in Philippians 4:13. Here contentment is not pride in needing nothing, but being satisfied with food and covering (6:8) because God gives "all things in rich supply" (6:17).

a: We carried nothing into the world
p: Job: 'Naked I came out from my mother's womb.' Polycarp's letter has wording very close to this verse and 6:10.
b: The thought is Job's: "Naked I came out from my mother's womb, / and naked I will return there" (Job 1:21), and Ecclesiastes 5:15. Jesus' rich fool learned the same (Luke 12:20). Polycarp's Letter to the Philippians, from the first half or the middle of the second century, has wording very close to this verse and 6:10: "the love of money is the root of all evils" and "as we brought nothing into the world, so we can carry nothing out" (chapter 4, in the old English translation). Scholars rate his use of 1 Timothy from a "high probability" (Holmes) to "almost certain" (Berding) and "certain" (Hartog), as Downs and Rogan (2016) report; if he used it, the letter was known by his time.

a: A root of every kind of evil is the love of money
p: The saying is not 'money is the root of all evil.' It is love of money, and 'a root' of every kind of evil.
b: The popular "money is the root of all evil" misquotes the verse twice. The subject is philargyria, "love of silver," not money itself, which the letter tells the rich to use generously (6:17-18). And the Greek has no article: "a root." "Of all the evils" probably means every kind of evil, not every single evil. The KJV's "the root of all evil" helped the misquotation along. Polycarp's letter has the saying in almost the same words (see the note at 6:7). The overseer must be "free from the love of money" (3:3).
orig: ῥίζα γὰρ πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐστιν ἡ φιλαργυρία

p: The Old Testament title of Moses, Elijah, Elisha and the prophets, here given to Timothy.
b: In the Old Testament "man of God" is a title for Moses (Deuteronomy 33:1), Samuel (1 Samuel 9:6), Elijah and Elisha (1 Kings 17:18; 2 Kings 4:9) and other prophets. By calling Timothy this, Paul sets him in that line: a person who belongs to God and speaks for him. 2 Timothy 3:17 uses it of anyone trained by Scripture.

a: Compete in the good contest of the faith
p: Agōnizou ton kalon agōna: an athlete's words. The KJV's 'fight the good fight' hides the games.
b: Agōn was the word for an athletic contest at the games, and also a struggle in general; the verb is the one in 4:10 ("struggle"). The KJV's famous "Fight the good fight" turned it into a battle, but the picture is the stadium: a race or a wrestling match with a prize ("grab hold of eternal life"). 2 Timothy 4:7 uses the same phrase at the end of Paul's life. Compare the soldier picture in 1:18.

p: At his baptism, at his ordination, or before a court? Each is possible.
b: "The good confession before many witnesses" may be (1) Timothy's confession of faith at his baptism, made before the gathered church (compare Romans 10:9-10); (2) his commitment at his ordination (4:14); or (3) a testimony before a court in a time of trial. The next verse links it to Jesus' own "good confession in front of Pontius Pilate," which favors a confession made under pressure, or at least sets Jesus as its model.

p: The only mention of Pilate in the letters in Paul's name. Later creeds kept him: Jesus suffered 'under Pontius Pilate'.
b: Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea who sentenced Jesus. This is the only place in the letters in Paul's name where he is named. The Greek epi Pontiou Pilatou can mean "before Pilate" or "in the time of Pilate." Jesus' confession was his testimony at his trial: "This is why I have been born, and this is why I have come into the world: to be a witness for the truth" (John 18:37). The Apostles' and Nicene Creeds later fixed Pilate's name in Christian worship, tying the faith to a real time in history.

p: Epiphaneia: the shining forth of a god or a king. The Pastorals' word for Christ's coming.
b: Epiphaneia means a coming into view, a manifestation. Greeks used it for a god showing himself to help his worshipers, and for a ruler's state visit; one Syrian king took the title "Epiphanes," "(God) Made Visible." The Pastorals use it for Christ's return (here; 2 Timothy 4:1, 8; Titus 2:13) and also for his first coming (2 Timothy 1:10). Paul's earlier letters say parousia, "coming" (1 Thessalonians 4:15). The site renders epiphaneia "appearing" throughout.

a: the King of those who reign and the Lord of those who rule
p: A Jewish title of God; Revelation gives it to the Lamb. Under the emperors it was a pointed claim.
b: The Greek reads, literally, "the King of those who are kings and Lord of those who are lords." Deuteronomy calls the LORD "the God of gods and the Lord of lords" (Deuteronomy 10:17), and Daniel's king praises a "Lord of kings" (Daniel 2:47). Revelation gives the title to the Lamb: "King of kings and Lord of lords" (Revelation 19:16; compare Revelation 17:14). Here it is God's. "The blessed one, the only Ruler" makes the same claim: in a world of emperors called lord and savior, there is one Ruler.

a: He alone has life that cannot die
p: Athanasia, 'deathlessness': God has it by nature; believers 'put it on' at the resurrection.
b: Athanasia means not being subject to death. God "alone" has it, in himself and by nature. Paul says that human beings receive it as a gift at the resurrection: "this thing that dies has to put on immortality" (1 Corinthians 15:53). So the verse has been used against the idea that the human soul is immortal by nature, and by others only to stress that all life comes from God. The light "no one can come near" echoes God's word to Moses: "no human being can see me and stay alive" (Exodus 33:20).

p: The church in Ephesus had wealthy members, patrons who hosted and funded it.
b: Ephesus was a rich port, and the church had wealthy members as well as slaves (6:1) and poor widows (5:3). The rich likely hosted the church in their houses and paid for its needs, as patrons did for clubs and cities. Paul does not tell them to give everything away; he tells them where to put their hope, and to become "rich in good works" (6:18). "Rich ... in rich supply ... rich in good works": the repeated word turns wealth into generosity.

p: Parathēkē: property left in someone's safekeeping. The faith is a deposit to be kept, not changed.
b: Parathēkē was a legal term for money or goods handed to a trusted person to keep safe and return intact. Here it is the good news and its teaching, entrusted to Timothy. The site renders the word "deposit" in both letters to Timothy. 2 Timothy uses the image twice (2 Timothy 1:12, 14), and 2 Timothy 2:2 tells him to pass it to faithful people who will teach others. Churches read the image differently: as the faith handed down in Scripture alone, or in Scripture and the church's living tradition. See the card at 3:15.

a: the knowledge that wrongly bears that name
p: Gnōsis became the name of the second-century Gnostics. Is the verse aimed at them, even at Marcion?
b: Tēs pseudōnymou gnōseōs, "the falsely named knowledge." In the second century, teachers called Gnostics (from gnōsis, "knowledge") claimed secret knowledge for the spiritual few, and Irenaeus fought them with this letter's words (see 1:4). "Counterclaims" is antitheseis, "Antitheses," which was the title of a book by Marcion, who set the Old Testament against the gospel. Some scholars therefore think the Pastorals were written partly against Marcion, around the middle of the second century. Others answer that "knowledge" was already a slogan at Corinth (1 Corinthians 8:1) and that antithesis is an ordinary word for an opposing argument.

p: The last word is plural, 'with you all': a letter to Timothy that the whole church was meant to hear.
b: The closing blessing uses the plural "you," as in 2 Timothy 4:22 and Titus 3:15. The letter is addressed to Timothy, but it was written to be read to the church: its rules about widows, elders and the rich were meant to be heard by widows, elders and the rich. Later copies changed it to the singular, "with you," to fit the address (see the variant).
